talks.title: Keynote
talks.teaser: Reframes software security as a business conversation about adversaries, risk, budget and the skills practitioners need next.
talks.summary:
The keynote argues that software security practitioners should think about software trust over the next decade and learn to explain their work in the terms a business uses. The speaker traces the industry's history, from firewalls and intrusion prevention through early paid code reviews and static analysis, and then argues that the usual vocabulary of threats and controls does not reach executives, who talk about customers, products and revenue.

The middle of the talk focuses on adversaries. The speaker suggests building attacker personas, using bug bounty results and external attack surface findings as signals, and linking vulnerabilities to the adversaries likely to exploit them rather than to raw severity scores. A risk matrix is recast around negative impact and the level of effort and cost to mitigate, which makes it easier to request budget. Other suggestions include setting acceptable thresholds, tracking measures such as whether teams feel more capable after security interactions and how often known issues become incidents, and presenting the case to a CFO in financial numbers.

The closing section lists skills the speaker expects to matter: checking the output of AI tools, threat intelligence, data storytelling, secure coding training and security architecture, which is described as an open gap. The talk ends with an invitation to a community survey and a dashboard toolkit. The practical takeaway is to describe risk in financial terms and to study the customers and attackers around a product.

talks.title: From Zero to ISO 27k Compliance
talks.teaser: Shows how a small company mapped its controls with the Secure Controls Framework and open-source tools toward ISO 27001 certification.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a sales story. A large healthcare prospect asked a small security software company for ISO 27001 evidence it did not hold, and the deal was lost. That loss pushed the company to pursue certification. The speakers explain why ISO 27001 was chosen over SOC 2 for a small organization: it is more objective, it covers legal and regulatory requirements, and its attestation cost is far lower.

The middle section covers the method. Rather than treating each framework as a separate audit, the team used the Secure Controls Framework, a free common-control catalogue mapped to more than 200 standards, to avoid audit fatigue. They loaded it into an open-source GRC platform, filtered it down to the relevant controls, and scored maturity levels instead of a simple pass or fail. Generative AI helped draft policies, procedures and test objectives, and free diagramming software covered process flows. On AWS, native services such as Inspector, Security Hub, GuardDuty, CloudTrail and CloudWatch served as evidence sources, although the presenters noted that much of their output needs manual filtering.

The closing part covers next steps. The team was looking for an auditor with small-company, AWS and CI/CD experience, and it was aiming for an audit the following year. The main takeaway is that mapping existing practices to a common control set and documenting them can cut effort, but the result still needs human review and expert judgment.

talks.title: It's a Bird, It's a Plane, It's A.I.
talks.teaser: Surveys how AI and large language models can help or harm security, with live chatbot demos built on open tools.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a tour of AI history, using books and films to separate general artificial intelligence from narrower systems built for specific jobs. The speaker argues that security work sits somewhere between art and science, and that practitioners should work alongside these tools rather than dismiss them. Early material explains how large language models predict the next word from training data, with human feedback shaping the results.

The middle section turns to practical concerns and tooling. Bias and hallucinations are presented as limits to plan around rather than reasons to ignore the technology. Open options are highlighted, including a local model runner, a public model hub, and a framework for linking models to external APIs, as ways to keep data off hosted services. Live demos follow: a plain chatbot that reveals its provider, a persona-driven bot, a bot grounded with event details through retrieval, and one that calls a file-hash reputation lookup through a function interface. A final demo has a model review C code for a buffer overflow and suggest a fix.

The closing point is that every integration is dual-use. Exposed functions and APIs can leak data or be abused if no access controls sit between the model and the backend, and attackers can run unrestricted local models to produce malicious code. For practitioners, the takeaway is to treat LLM-connected features as part of the application attack surface, test them like any other input path, and build hands-on familiarity with these tools now.

talks.title: Who IAM – a Closer Look at IAM and CIAM
talks.teaser: Compares workforce and customer identity and access management systems, covering their shared building blocks and key differences.
talks.summary:
The speakers open by framing identity and access management (IAM) as a long-standing pillar of information security. They explain that the growth of online services has pushed IAM systems to evolve, leaving buyers with many variants to choose from. They sort these systems into two families: workforce IAM, which serves employees, contractors and partners inside an organisation, and customer IAM (CIAM), which serves external consumers, citizens and clients of a service provider.

They then walk through the core IAM functions, including directories, provisioning, authentication, single sign-on, authorization, lifecycle management, and logging and auditing. Next they show how CIAM handles registration, social login, progressive profiling, consent capture and adaptive authentication, using illustrative examples from insurance and tax services. The comparison covers what the two share, such as multi-factor authentication, federation, API protection and account lifecycle. It also covers where they diverge: role-based policies and approval workflows on the workforce side, versus self-service, user experience, branding and hard-to-predict traffic on the customer side.

The closing part contrasts security posture, privacy obligations and trust assumptions. Workforce IAM leans toward least privilege under HR and IT control, while CIAM balances protection against friction and must meet privacy regulations such as GDPR. The takeaway is that the two designs serve different goals, so teams choosing an IAM platform should first decide whether access control or user experience matters more.

talks.title: A visual journey to reverse-engineering the Enigma Machine - preventing MITM
talks.teaser: Traces how the Enigma machine's rotors, reflector and plugboard worked, then rebuilds it with serverless functions.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a tour of early substitution ciphers, from the reversed-alphabet Atbash and Caesar shifts to tap code and Morse, and explains why frequency analysis could break them. It then presents the Enigma machine as a commercial answer to that weakness, developed after the First World War to protect messages from interception before military forces adopted it.

The middle section takes the machine apart. It covers the keyboard and lamp board, three rotors that step like an odometer after each keypress, a reflector that lets the same settings both encrypt and decrypt, and a plugboard on military models. Using a simplified rotor diagram, the speaker shows how the signal path changes with each press and estimates the size of the configuration space. Daily settings were distributed in code books, and the initial setting was sent twice to catch errors.

To finish, the speaker rebuilds the machine as a state machine, with one serverless function per component, a workflow service ordering the steps, an API and a small web interface. A live demo with audience-chosen settings encrypts a short word, and changing a single setting turns the output into unreadable text. The session closes with code for the lookup logic and a Q&A on why code books were harder to capture than the machines themselves, and on how codebreakers exploited the fact that a letter could never encode to itself.

talks.title: Wolfi: A Secure-by-Default Distro for Curing Container CVE Chaos
talks.teaser: Shows how the Wolfi distribution and its apko and melange tools build minimal container images with far fewer known CVEs.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the problem: popular base and application images from public registries often carry hundreds of known vulnerabilities, driven by large dependency trees and outdated packages. The speaker argues that most of a modern software stack is open-source code that teams rarely examine, and that routine cleanup such as running package updates and removing archives barely reduces the CVE count. Scan comparisons across popular language and application images illustrate the gap against purpose-built images.

The middle of the talk surveys how containers are commonly built, from standard Dockerfiles to distroless approaches and tools such as ko, Jib and Bazel. Distroless images still have gaps, since some ship with shells, package managers or vulnerable binaries. Wolfi is presented as a rolling, container-focused Linux distribution that uses the APK package format, publishes SBOMs and signed attestations, and rebuilds packages quickly when upstream patches land. The live demo shows a Python Flask application built the Docker way, then as a drop-in Wolfi image, and then assembled with apko from packages built with melange.

The takeaway for practitioners is that a declarative, reproducible build pipeline can produce smaller images with fewer known vulnerabilities and a verifiable build history. Debugging is best done before an image reaches production, using the exact package and image digest. The talk also notes that the tools run as standalone Go binaries without a container runtime for the build step.

talks.title: Cybersecurity Architecture in the Age of Covid
talks.teaser: Explains how pandemic-driven remote work strained security architecture and which controls help modernize it.
talks.summary:
The talk starts with traditional perimeter security, where a firewall guards a trusted internal network. Shared local admin passwords and implicit trust between hosts and accounts let an intruder move freely once inside. The speaker argues that cloud services, IoT devices and partner connections had already weakened that model before 2020. When offices closed, remote access systems sized for a small group suddenly served nearly everyone.

The middle section frames defense around time: prevention must hold long enough for detection and response to act. Suggested controls include purple team exercises covering remote-user scenarios, asset inventory, tiered and segmented networks, hardware-key MFA for critical users, virtual desktops, dynamic access control on VPNs, and data loss prevention across cloud apps. Logs should be kept in a self-managed SIEM for at least a year, and EDR quarantine should be tested before it is needed.

The closing part covers end-user habits, separating home networks, and the return-to-office debate, which raises employee monitoring and privacy questions for legal teams. The speaker presents these as mitigations rather than one fixed architecture and urges practitioners to choose tools that fit their own environment and budget.

talks.title: Invited
talks.teaser: Shows how zero trust principles and browser-based access can protect internal web applications and reduce exposed attack surface.
talks.summary:
The talk, given by a security consultant from an Austin firm, argues that zero trust principles can shrink the exposure of internal web applications and lower ransomware risk. The speaker traces zero trust from its 2010 origins through NIST SP 800-207 and the CISA maturity model, outlining its five pillars (identity, devices, network, applications and workloads, and data) and the staged progression from traditional to optimal. He stresses that adoption is incremental, that organizations should start with an assessment and quick wins, and that vendor choice depends on the organization.

The middle of the talk is a walkthrough of a cloud-delivered zero trust service. Browser-based access to internal tools is placed behind single sign-on with MFA, and a small outbound tunnel on an internal machine exposes resources without opening inbound firewall ports. Temporary access for third parties can be approved through a one-time request, and the demo included browser-based SSH and an attempt at reaching a scanner, although one live session did not respond.

The closing section covers developer access, where DNS filtering, HTTP inspection, malware scanning and device posture checks are used to control risky browsing on corporate laptops. The main takeaway is to remove unnecessary public exposure of RDP, management interfaces and legacy VPN entry points, and to map the effort to existing compliance requirements.

talks.title: Small Language Models for Application Security - Beyond ChatGPT
talks.teaser: Shows how small open-source language models can support design reviews, threat modeling and code review in appsec.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the shift from hosted commercial language models to small open-source ones that an organization can run privately for sensitive security work. The speaker traces how these models developed since the transformer architecture, then introduces an internal five-level maturity scale for language model applications, from simple chat to retrieval-backed and agent-style designs.

The core of the talk maps model capabilities such as summarization, question answering and classification onto appsec work: security design reviews, threat modeling and code review. In each case the model handles the reading and first-pass analysis while a person stays in the loop to check the output. Good inputs matter, so the speaker recommends structured documentation, text-based diagrams and descriptive pull requests.

The build section covers model selection, a low temperature setting, memory needs for loading models, and a simple stack of Python, Hugging Face Transformers, a retrieval index and a Gradio interface triggered by a CI webhook. A live demo reviewed a real public pull request. The takeaways: open models avoid sending code to third parties, they can keep costs predictable compared with hosted API spending, and they need logging so reviewers can audit decisions.

talks.title: PASTA Threat Modeling & Leveraging IR, Threat Intelligence as Means for Tactical Pen Test
talks.teaser: Shows how incident data and threat intelligence can ground a PASTA threat model that guides adversarial testing.
talks.summary:
The talk focuses on stage four of PASTA, the risk-centric threat modeling method, and on how a threat library can be backed by evidence rather than kept as a compliance checkbox. The speaker argues that alerts from firewalls, web application firewalls and endpoint tools, along with industry advisories and incident postmortems, are usually triaged and then forgotten. Feeding them back into the model gives adversarial testers a reason to target particular components.

Two case studies anchor the argument. The first covers a connected children's toy whose companion app, cloud APIs and backend database were linked to a breach after a staging environment held real user records. The second covers an energy-sector SaaS used to monitor oil well production, where a misconfigured tenant management page gave access to a client's well sites and production data. For each, the speaker walks through how a threat such as data theft, sabotage or tampering maps to assets, vulnerabilities, attacks and countermeasures in an attack tree.

The closing takeaway is that threat intelligence should be operationalized into the model rather than merely subscribed to, and that a threat-to-attack blueprint lets a pentester test for abuse cases the business actually cares about. The speaker recommends building the model collaboratively with developers and product owners, using frameworks such as ATT&CK and OWASP ASVS for mapping, and applying the approach to both legacy and new products.

talks.title: Easy-bake IR - Automated incident response using the power of APIs
talks.teaser: Shows how scripts and APIs can speed up a breach investigation, from leaked credentials to email, cloud logs and EDR indicators.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the chaos of a breach where every team has a different theory and existing controls have missed the early stages of the attack. The speaker recommends working backwards from the data that is still available, and stresses preserving volatile evidence before anyone reboots, rebuilds or patches systems. He compares the SANS PICERL and NIST incident response lifecycles, noting that investigation and containment often loop back on each other, and points to breach reports and threat trend studies as sources for planning.

The middle of the talk follows a fictional case involving a recently acquired business unit. A breach-exposure lookup of employee addresses points to one user with a history of phishing failures. The mailbox export is hashed and logged to a verifiable evidence store, then parsed for sender domain reputation, domain registration age, URLs, IP reputation and password-reset keywords. An interview with the user, combined with CloudTrail events pulled through the AWS API, reveals a changed database master password, many new access keys and logins through a suspicious VPN. Apache Tika then extracts text from attachments so a redaction engine can count personal identifiers such as Social Security numbers, and the malicious indicators are uploaded to an EDR platform through its API.

The takeaway is that a notebook of reusable scripts can shorten triage and leave a documented evidence trail, provided responsibilities are separated between requesting, approving and analysing data. Responders should involve HR and legal early, account for regional rules on employee data, and avoid partial investigations that leave attackers able to return.

talks.title: Infrastructure as Remote Code Execution: How to abuse Terraform to elevate access
talks.teaser: Shows how Terraform pipelines can be abused to run code, leak credentials and escalate cloud privileges, plus defenses.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces Terraform as an infrastructure-as-code tool that keeps a state file describing deployed resources. The speaker argues that this state file and the surrounding pipeline are sensitive targets, because state often holds secrets such as database passwords and receives far less logging and scrutiny than a dedicated secrets manager.

The middle of the talk covers ways someone with pipeline access can go beyond normal deployment. Debug logging can expose temporary cloud credentials in pipeline output. Built-in provisioners such as remote-exec and local-exec can run arbitrary scripts on servers or on the Terraform host, and the external data source can run custom scripts as well. Data sources can also pull sensitive parameters into plans and logs, and the instance metadata service can be queried from the Terraform host. Provider code is a large third-party dependency, and values marked as unknown until apply can hide resources from policy checks written against the plan.

For defenders, the talk recommends pattern-matching rules in Semgrep to block provisioners, policy-as-code checks with Sentinel or OPA, and tightly scoped IAM roles for the pipeline, split by team rather than one shared administrator. It also suggests restricting where the role can be used through IAM conditions, enforcing IMDSv2, reviewing code and modules, and alerting on changes to the pipeline's permissions. The takeaway is that Terraform is valuable for standardizing cloud infrastructure, but it needs least-privilege access and close review of what it executes.

talks.title: Navigating Security pitfalls during M&A: Playbooks & Strategies for doing acquisitions right
talks.teaser: Shows how a security team can run checks before and after an acquisition without slowing the deal down.
talks.summary:
The talk explains how a security team can take part in mergers and acquisitions, drawing on the speakers' experience across roughly two dozen deals at a large tech company. It starts with the deal lifecycle: corporate development finds a target, and security joins during due diligence, a window that often lasts only a few weeks. The speakers explain why the goal is to avoid inheriting a breach, pointing to well-known cases where intrusions surfaced after closing.

The middle section walks through a pre-acquisition workflow. A questionnaire collects asset lists, exposed services and architecture diagrams, and an outside firm runs a short penetration test so the target does not have to share its source code directly with the buyer. Findings are passed to the business for risk-based decisions. For larger deals, a compromise assessment deploys endpoint monitoring for several weeks to look for active intrusions. Post-close integration is sized by model, such as an equity hire, full, limited or delayed integration. The speakers also describe practical hurdles, including missing endpoint management, shadow IT found through finance records, and lost access to cloud accounts when staff leave.

The closing takeaways are to define exit criteria, agree on shared ownership of critical accounts, keep playbooks flexible, and communicate early with leadership and the acquired team. In the question period, an audience member suggested embedding a dedicated security person in a deal for about a year, which the speakers said was a useful idea.

talks.title: Top Gun's unsung hero - a surprising lesson for CI/CD security
talks.teaser: Uses a Vietnam-era Navy story to frame how CI/CD pipelines can be secured through flow control, log correlation, and alerting.
talks.summary:
The talk opens in 1968, when the U.S. Navy's losses over Vietnam had mounted to nearly a thousand aircraft. An investigation traced the problem to flawed missile procurement and to pilots who relied on rigid tactics that the enemy had learned to predict. The speaker highlights the officer who was tasked with setting up the fighter weapons school, who chose to train pilots to expect failure and adapt quickly. The speaker then ties that lesson to securing software delivery.

Applying this to CI/CD, the speaker walks through a pipeline from source code to production and lists core properties to control: branch protection and code review, pipeline-as-code, curated package sources, and policy checks at deploy time. Cross-system bypasses are the main example, such as a feature branch publishing packages to a production location, or a main-branch build pulling dependencies straight from the internet. Because no single system's logs reveal these flows, the speaker recommends collecting build, source control, and package logs in one place, enriching them with lookup data such as which branches are protected, and building alerts with playbooks. Direct commits to protected branches and freestyle Jenkins jobs are offered as easy starting detections.

The closing argument separates quick tactical fixes from strategic root-cause investigations, which are worth doing when events repeat. The speaker also argues that encouraging engineers to report pipeline weaknesses turns them into useful alert sources. In the Q&A, the speaker favors guardrails, such as avoiding unsupported or vulnerable build tool versions, over strict tool standardization.

talks.title: Unveiling the Vulnerabilities: Hacking Cloud Native Apps and Discovering the Silver Lining
talks.teaser: Shows how misconfigured Cognito, S3 buckets, OAuth flows and Lambda APIs expose cloud-hosted web applications to takeover.
talks.summary:
This talk covers how to attack cloud-hosted web applications from a black-box position, where the tester has no cloud account and the cloud pieces of an app are not obvious. The speaker argues that traditional scanners miss these issues, so testers first need to find which cloud services an app relies on. Fingerprinting looks at URL patterns, response headers and bundled JavaScript for signs of storage buckets, Cognito pools and API gateways. A Burp extension built for this purpose, Cloud Asset Watcher, flags such assets while you browse.

The middle section covers the main weak spots. For Cognito, the checks include open sign-up, mutable user attributes, unverified emails and unauthenticated identity pool roles that issue AWS credentials. For OAuth, it covers loose redirect URI checks, missing state validation and response-type switching. One takeover case shows how trusting a mutable email attribute, instead of a stable subject identifier, lets an attacker log in as another user. Public buckets, wildcard IAM policies and role-passing abuse lead to privilege escalation, while API and Lambda examples include leaky older API versions, mass assignment and unsafe code in functions.

The closing advice is to inventory cloud resources, review IAM policies for broad permissions, key identity decisions on immutable identifiers, validate redirect URIs strictly and avoid undocumented APIs. Practitioners should also watch billing and cloud audit logs for signs of misuse.

talks.title: Securing Generative AI
talks.teaser: Shows how familiar security APIs like redaction, threat intel and access control can be inserted into generative AI chat flows.
talks.summary:
Rob Truesdell frames generative AI security through the "alternate 1985" from Back to the Future Part II: a warped present full of new problems, including data leakage, manipulated models, legal questions and attacks on prompts. His point is that most of these have familiar answers from enterprise and network security. The place to apply them is the API layer between users, the chat interface, the model and surrounding components. He lists data classification and filtering, threat intelligence lookups, strong authentication, fine-grained access control, tamper-resistant audit logging and digital signing of content.

The middle of the talk shows a simple chat app built on the OpenAI API. Prompts pass through a redaction service that removes items such as Social Security numbers before reaching the model, and responses are checked for malicious domains and URLs before they go back to the user, with suspicious links defanged or removed. Every exchange is logged. He concedes that pattern matching only catches known formats and cannot adapt to new inputs on its own. For authorization, he recommends checks in the orchestration layer before a vector database is queried, and suggests attribute-based policies that consider factors such as time of day or employee tenure. Audience questions touched on explainability and detecting prompt injection, where extracting indicators for threat intelligence lookups was the current best option.

He closes by calling this no silver bullet. Audit logging and data protection can be deployed today, while access control and content authenticity are achievable with more custom work. A shared trust framework for generative AI is still in progress and needs community samples. The takeaway for practitioners is that the controls already exist and the API layer is a logical place to add them.

talks.title: 3cx: lessons learned
talks.teaser: Walks through the 3CX supply chain compromise and the controls that could have caught the trojanized update.
talks.summary:
The talk examines the 3CX incident, in which a VoIP software vendor shipped a trojanized desktop update to thousands of customers, some of whom then reported compromised internal systems. The speaker traces how the problem unfolded, from an endpoint security product flagging the software as suspicious, to community threads where the flag was dismissed as a false positive, to the vendor later confirming the malicious code. The incident is placed alongside earlier supply chain events such as SolarWinds and Codecov, and the speaker argues the pattern keeps repeating.

The middle section explains why common defenses fell short. Antivirus engines often rely on reputation and on partial scanning of large files, and sandboxes can stop at a fixed depth of nested archives or miss behavior that only appears later. The talk recommends reproducible builds so that artifacts can be compared bit for bit against an expected result, and diffing each release against the previous one to surface new network calls or unexpected behavior. It also covers typosquatted packages in public repositories and a Windows trust weakness, where a partially signed package can still validate.

For practitioners, the takeaways are to verify that build pipelines have not been tampered with, to test whether a release will trigger antivirus alerts before it ships, to keep a clear decision-maker ready during an incident, and to plan how customers will be told what happened. The speaker also suggests planting canary secrets to detect misuse of leaked credentials.

talks.title: A new recipe for security risk evaluation
talks.teaser: Presents an enhanced risk formula that folds CVSS factors into ISO 27005-based assessment without double-counting.
talks.summary:
Security scans often return long lists of findings, and product teams need a way to decide which ones to fix first. The talk explains that a CVSS base score measures a vulnerability's technical severity in isolation, not its risk to a particular product. It then outlines a risk model used for many years, based on ISO 27005, in which vulnerabilities sit on supporting assets and threats aim at business assets.

The middle of the talk covers the open-source risk assessment tool built around that model. The tool walks users through assets, threats, likelihood questions, and controls, then produces a numeric score. The recent revision draws likelihood factors from the OWASP calculator and borrows two CVSS v3 factors, user interaction and scope, while avoiding overlap with criteria already counted. Those factors act as multipliers, and their constants were tuned by simulation against historical assessments.

A product management example shows the output in practice: a feature with a medium risk was dropped once the team weighed it against the small share of users who had requested it. The takeaway is to judge risk in business context rather than by severity alone. The speaker presented the new formula as still under evaluation and invited feedback from the community.

talks.title: All About the Benjamins: Building a Business-Critical Bug Bounty Program
talks.teaser: Shows how Yahoo's bug bounty program secured lasting funding by proving its business value to internal stakeholders.
talks.summary:
The talk traces the history of Yahoo's bug bounty program, from an early disclosure episode and a small AOL-era recognition page through the merger of several company programs into one public program around 2017. The speaker describes a series of live hacking events in different countries, including a pilot that produced little activity, and explains how later events in San Francisco, Buenos Aires and New York showed that in-person sessions could sustain researcher engagement for weeks. Team-based formats and brand-focused events were also tested.

By 2020, after years of payouts, legal, finance, HR, executives and internal audit began asking whether the program was worth its cost and how it was controlled. The response covered sanctions screening of payees, vendor and contract reviews, and a cost-benefit model that multiplied an estimated breach cost by an assumed probability and the number of relevant bugs. Payment workflows were split into separate steps with independent approvals, and policies were written on whether former employees and contractors could take part.

The main takeaways are to identify every stakeholder early, think like an auditor so that processes are repeatable, and connect security work to business value. Consistent payout rules and operational runbooks keep researchers trusting the program, and a team should have solid product security hygiene before launching, since a new program attracts heavy traffic.

talks.title: Five Pillars of Security Automation
talks.teaser: Looks back at a decade of API security automation and sets out five pillars for building a lasting program.
talks.summary:
Oleg Gryb, who works in product security at Block and previously led security teams at Visa and Samsung, reviews how API security automation has changed over ten years and what he expects to matter next. He starts with the obstacles his teams faced: friction between security and delivery in large organisations, scan results that need manual triage, APIs that cannot be crawled the way web applications can, and many proprietary authentication schemes that scanners must be told about explicitly.

He contrasts his earlier setup, built on mostly free tools and a very small team, with a later one. The newer setup pairs Burp extensions and an out-of-band collaborator server with a payload generator that replays valid API call sequences through a proxy so active scanning can run. He notes that active scans break when they change system state, and that findings were held back from product teams until someone had verified them. He also surveys newer discovery approaches, including traffic mirroring with TLS decryption and eBPF-based agents.

The core of the talk is his five pillars: API discovery, an inventory of endpoints and their metadata, reusable templates, testing tools that pull targets from that inventory, and a shared framework so testers do not restart from scratch. He closes with a case study in which a server-side request forgery issue was dismissed as intended behaviour. He measured the impact of unrestricted outbound connections, which led to rate limiting being adopted. His takeaway is that persuading developers with measurable impact matters as much as the scanning itself.

talks.title: AT&T Cybersecurity Insights Report: Edge Ecosystem
talks.teaser: Presents survey findings on edge computing use cases, endpoints, and attack concerns across seven industry verticals.
talks.summary:
The talk presents the AT&T Cybersecurity Insights Report, a vendor-neutral study now in its twelfth edition. The research drew on a global field survey of 1,418 respondents in security, IT, application development and line-of-business roles, supplemented by qualitative input from industry experts. Seven verticals were covered, including healthcare, retail, finance, manufacturing, energy, transportation and public sector.

The speaker defined edge computing as software-defined workloads hosted close to where data is generated and consumed, managed through a distributed model. Respondents reported endpoints beyond the usual laptops and phones, such as robots, wearables and autonomous drones. Key findings included security budgets planned roughly on par with applications, network and strategy, heavy reliance on outside advisers, and an average of about 71 percent bringing in third-party help once systems reached production. Respondents ranked denial of service as their top attack concern while rating patching and DoS defenses as low priority, which the speaker described as legacy thinking.

The closing section walked through example use cases such as video-based quality inspection, smart building management and real-time fraud protection, and stressed that a widening attack surface makes resilience essential. The practical advice was to start from the business outcome, align internal stakeholders, bring in trusted partners and plan for dynamic cyber resilience. The vertical reports and printed copies of the report were offered to attendees.

talks.title: Enhancing ReactJS Application Security: XSS Scripting and Client-Side Defense
talks.teaser: Surveys XSS and client-side defenses for ReactJS apps, plus API, token and access control risks developers face.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with where security bugs come from in modern software: developer-written code, third-party libraries, and cloud configuration. The speaker argues for security gates in the devops pipeline, automated testing on every commit, requirements tailored to each team from the ASVS, and threat modeling generated from API traffic rather than whiteboard interviews.

The middle section is a broad tour of web and API defenses. Topics include session cookies and security headers, sandboxed iframes, CORS behavior once applications move to microservices, REST pitfalls such as sensitive data in URLs, server-side request forgery, JSON parsing and deserialization, JWT signature checks and token revocation, SQL injection through input that passes validation, CSRF, file upload handling, prompt injection in LLM applications, and the OWASP Top 10. Broken access control is highlighted as a business logic gap that common scanners miss.

For ReactJS specifically, the focus is cross-site scripting. The talk recommends context-appropriate output escaping, a sanitizer such as DOMPurify for user-authored HTML, and validating URL protocols before rendering links, since JavaScript URLs can bypass React's protections. The takeaway is that client-side code needs its own defenses, and that authorization checks belong in the data layer rather than in hardcoded roles.

talks.title: Tenants for Going at DevSecOps Speed
talks.teaser: Shows how to build a DevSecOps program that keeps pace with many apps and tool outputs without burning out the team.
talks.summary:
The talk addresses someone newly handed a DevSecOps or product security role, facing many applications and a pile of tool output with a small team. Matt Tesauro argues that two foundations come first: an early initial assessment that sets a baseline for measuring progress, and a single source of truth that consolidates findings and adapts as the business changes. He points to OWASP DefectDojo as a platform built for this job.

The core of the talk is a four-stage pipeline of intake, triage, testing, and delivery. Intake improves when teams stop re-requesting the same data and when routine checks run automatically ahead of time. Triage sorts work into a few concrete effort levels based on business criticality and tool accuracy. Testing depends on cadence, since audits, proactive scans, and urgent disclosures compete for the same people. New tools should run quietly before they gate CI/CD, because false positives that break builds quickly erode support. Delivery means speaking each stakeholder's language, whether that is issue tracker entries for developers or charts for executives.

The closing advice is to define scope, build a workflow, iterate constantly, and let feedback shape the program rather than dictating it. Automating repetitive work matters because people remain the scarcest resource.

talks.title: Beyond Vulnerabilities: Analyzing Behaviors to Spot Malware in Your Release
talks.teaser: Shows how static behavior analysis and release diffs can flag malware hidden in software builds before customers receive it.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from a shift in thinking: the SolarWinds, Equifax and 3CX incidents show that a release can cause harm without containing any vulnerability. Vulnerability scanners look for flaws in code and do not assess what a program is meant to do, so they miss malicious additions. Build pipelines are also hard to lock down because they span many tools, runners and dependency sources.

The proposed approach is to analyze behaviors instead of only bugs. Static binary analysis unpacks a package layer by layer, down to compiled code, and maps that code to system effects such as starting processes, opening network sockets or changing security services. Dynamic sandboxing is slower and can be evaded by malware that stays dormant. The key idea is differential analysis: set a known-good release as a baseline and review the behaviors that are new in each later version. Examples from SolarWinds and 3CX showed new low-level calls and a partially validated digital signature in changed DLLs, and a backdoor injected at build time in a Black Hat demonstration added new network behaviors.

The talk closed with a Jenkins demo in which a static scan stage ran after each build. A modified sample web app that read a password file and sent it out produced eleven new behaviors in the diff. The takeaways are to automate the diff in CI/CD, define which behaviors each release should have, and fail builds on unexpected changes. Behavior comparison also helps check reproducible builds, where file hashes differ for harmless reasons.

talks.title: Reducing Alert Fatigue with Container Scans: Correlate, Prioritize and Filter Based on Usage
talks.teaser: Shows how runtime usage data and exploit maturity can narrow container and dependency scan findings to what matters.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a common scenario: an application built from twelve containers with about 400 packages, where a software composition analysis scan reports more than a hundred vulnerable components. Security teams want critical and high findings fixed, but development teams lack the capacity, and severity scores alone push effort toward issues that may never be reachable.

The speaker proposes a second generation of composition analysis that combines static scan output with runtime evidence. Six factors guide triage: runtime usage, reachability, exploit maturity, deployment topology, severity policy and applicability. A live demo on a multi-service sample banking application shows how filtering down to components that were actually loaded, then to those with known exploits, cuts a large list to a handful. In one Log4j example, only a few instances were both loaded and vulnerable. The talk also covers instrumentation options, including eBPF, user-space preloading and language agents, and notes that unused packages can be removed to shrink images and reduce debt.

The takeaway is to prioritise by demonstrated exposure rather than raw counts, give developers a short fix list, and track risk posture over time instead of vulnerability totals. Runtime data only reflects code that runs during the observation window, so the speaker recommends exercising applications through tests or canary deployments before trusting the baseline.

talks.title: System Assurance with the IoT Security Testing Guide
talks.teaser: Presents the OWASP IoT Security Testing Guide's models, tools and test case catalog for repeatable device penetration tests.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces the OWASP IoT Security Testing Guide, a methodology meant to make penetration tests of connected devices repeatable and comparable. The speaker notes that many device assessments arrive as static PDF reports that cannot be rerun, and that existing guides leave physical and authorization context underspecified.

The core of the talk is the guide's structure. A device model splits the target into components, from processing units and memory through firmware, interfaces and wireless links up to user interfaces. Two scoping axes then frame each engagement: physical access, ranging from remote through local and non-invasive to invasive lab work, and logical access, from unauthorized and low-privilege accounts up to high-privilege and manufacturer-level access. Test cases are listed per component with their required access levels, objectives, remediation notes and references, and are offered in checklist, markdown, spreadsheet and machine-readable formats. A worked example contrasts a wall-mounted commercial camera, where hardware-level cases drop out, with a consumer camera held in hand. Tooling ranges from firmware analysis toolkits to hardware debug interfaces such as JTAG and UART.

For practitioners, the takeaway is to define scope using both access axes so results can be repeated and compared over time. The project was in peer review and still in incubator stage, and the speaker invited contributions, especially for Bluetooth, Wi-Fi and other wireless modules and for lower-level boot and root-of-trust work.

talks.title: Advancing Your Threat Modeling Approaches in an Agile / DevOps World
talks.teaser: Explains how threat modeling can fit into agile and DevOps workflows through incremental, story-based and code-driven approaches.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a common complaint: teams practicing agile or DevOps often say they have no time for threat modeling. The speaker argues that threat modeling is a thinking exercise rather than a scan or code review, aimed at design flaws such as confusing authentication with authorization. He covers the basic parts of a threat model, including a system representation like a data flow diagram, identified threats, mitigations and prioritized risks, and references the four guiding questions from the Threat Modeling Manifesto.

The middle section focuses on fitting this work into fast-moving teams. Suggested approaches include building a baseline from whatever diagram already exists, adding threat discussion to sprint planning, and writing attacker or abuser stories next to user stories so that defenses and detection become acceptance criteria. He describes a large organization that used a short rapid risk assessment, triggered only when a change affects entry points, attack surface or sensitive data. He also surveys threat-modeling-as-code tools that generate data flow diagrams from annotated code or from Python, YAML and HCL definitions, and recommends modeling CI/CD pipelines with existing knowledge bases such as MITRE ATT&CK.

The closing portion touches on generative AI, which can help map components to likely threats but still needs human judgment to check the results. The speaker stresses that a threat model is never finished and should be revisited as features change. His practical takeaways are to start with what exists, keep sessions short, include operations and testing staff alongside developers, and treat privacy as a related area to study.

talks.title: The road to AppSec Maturity is through Unification
talks.teaser: Explains how unifying application and infrastructure security helps AppSec programs mature through shared visibility and workflows.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from the pressure modern software delivery puts on security teams. Agile development, microservices, open source, containers and infrastructure as code mean software ships more often and in more places, while scanning tools sit in silos. Approvals, triage and remediation follow-up often live in spreadsheets, email and chat. The speaker argues that application and infrastructure security are usually handled separately, even though they affect each other.

The middle of the talk presents a maturity model developed by a practitioner community, called S3M2 in the talk. It rates a program from one to five across people, process and technology. The speaker walks through what each level looks like, from ad hoc manual work to automated policy enforcement and real-time feedback loops. The model is meant for self-assessment rather than a fixed target, since a small organization may reasonably stay at a lower level. Recurring themes include visibility across assets, business context for prioritization, and enforcing service-level agreements across teams.

The closing section lists five capabilities a strong program needs: unified visibility across applications, cloud, containers and the supply chain; risk-based prioritization; remediation inside tools developers already use; automation that scales; and measurement through reporting and tracking. The main takeaway is that maturing an AppSec program depends on unifying tools, environments and workflows. A vendor platform is presented as one option for doing this, and the speaker notes that other approaches also work.

talks.title: Discovering and Empowering the Expert-Level Cybersecurity Talent Within Your Team
talks.teaser: Shows how a security team grew expert-level skills in-house by giving staff protected time to automate routine work.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from a hiring problem: expert-level security talent is hard to recruit, so the speaker argues organizations should grow it from existing staff. The speaker traces a personal path from systems administration into full-time security work, reaching principal architect level over about a decade as a state government employee. The core idea is a protected block of time each week, roughly one or two hours, for staff to find repetitive chores and automate or simplify them.

The approach was piloted internally under the name GSC, standing for grow, simplify and enhance. Participants propose a task, define requirements, and report to their manager monthly, with management removing blockers instead of micromanaging. Metrics are individual, and an exit gate requires documentation, training and a team vote confirming others can support the result before the next round begins. Examples included checking asset inventories across security tools for gaps, and replacing a manual phishing-results request with a self-service dashboard fed by automated data pulls.

After about four months, just under half the team had joined, and the phishing dashboard was roughly 70 percent complete. Progress was slower than hoped because of leave, incidents and executive requests. Takeaways include starting with small wins, expecting slow growth, avoiding direct comparisons between junior and senior staff, and offering recognition rather than penalties to those who opt out. Documentation and training keep the automation running after its creator moves on.

talks.title: The Monsters in Your Software Supply Chain That SCA Can't Find
talks.teaser: Explains why malware inserted during builds slips past SCA and AppSec tools, and what teams can do about it.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from the way software is now built: CI/CD pipelines, microservices and frequent releases have replaced slower waterfall processes, and that shift has widened the set of places an attacker can reach. The speaker argues that supply chain risk is growing for this reason, and that it affects organisations whether they write software or only consume it.

The middle section maps a typical development lifecycle, from developer tools and code repositories through build systems, CI orchestration and open source packages, to deployment. The speaker suggests that the finished build is the most useful point to check for tampering. He explains that common tools such as SAST, SCA, DAST, IAST and RASP are designed to find vulnerabilities, not malware, so they can miss attacks inserted during the build. Recent incidents, including SolarWinds, Codecov, CircleCI and 3CX, are used to show different entry points. Other risks covered include typosquatting, dependency reachability, the Log4j episode, and the need for accurate SBOMs that follow standard formats.

For practitioners, the closing advice is to stop relying on vendor questionnaires and on trust in updates. Teams should compare releases, verify packages, automate checks inside the CI/CD pipeline without slowing developers, and include supply chain vetting in procurement and acquisition due diligence. The talk ends with a homework task for attendees: review vendor security collateral with a critical eye.

talks.title: Building a Risk Based Vulnerability Management Program
talks.teaser: Shows how to build a risk-based vulnerability management program that a business can actually sustain.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the common ways vulnerability management programs fail. Teams left to their own devices end up with orphaned infrastructure and no clear owner, while strict, CVSS-driven mandates stall product delivery. Recurring prioritization meetings and pushing patching onto engineers also break down, especially when an urgent issue lands between planning cycles.

The approach presented sets default remediation timelines, such as 90, 30 and 7 days, then adjusts them using a likelihood and impact matrix tailored to the organization's own environment. Mitigations such as a WAF, a firewall in front of a system, or network segmentation can justify more time, and an internal risk rating can replace the severity stated in a penetration test report. A worked example involving a recent VMware vulnerability shows how an item moves through each step. Items that still cannot meet expectations escalate to senior leadership, who decide whether to accept the risk or fund the fix.

The takeaways centre on the security team informing risk decisions rather than owning them, feeding scanner output into sprint planning as a stack-ranked list, and monitoring exceptions as the main signal. The speaker acknowledges that the model is hard to scale to very large environments and suggests pairing a GRC function with a technical engineer. Bug bounty severity should also be aligned with what the program actually values.

talks.title: Security Safari: A Journey Through the Wilderness of Securing Budding Opensource Projects
talks.teaser: Gives open source maintainers a prescriptive set of CNCF security guidelines to apply to a new project from day one.
talks.summary:
The speakers open with the problem facing open source projects. Most companies depend on open source software, and incidents such as Log4j and Heartbleed show how much risk sits in dependencies nobody tracks. Maintainers of new projects face a large volume of security guidance from many bodies, so it is hard to know where to begin. The talk presents a set of bite-sized guidelines, prepared by the CNCF technical advisory group for security, meant to be applied when a repository is first opened.

The guidance is organised into steps. The first covers the source repository itself: strong authentication and access keys, defined code owners, pull request review for every change, and branch protection, including the setting that stops administrators from bypassing the rules. Contributor-facing steps follow, such as issue templates and automated checks like secret scanning and static analysis. A living self-assessment document records the project's goals, actors, compliance needs and secure development practices. In the live demo, the presenters start from a CNCF project template, configure branch protection, add an OpenSSF Scorecard workflow through GitHub Actions, enable private vulnerability reporting, add a security policy file, and set up gitignore and license files.

The later part of the guidance covers public security awareness, vulnerability disclosure and embargo handling, communication with upstream and downstream users, and incident triage with defined severity levels. The main takeaway is to start with the basics on day one. Scorecard results point to what to fix next, and checks that do not fit a given project can be disabled. The speakers ask security practitioners for feedback on the guidelines.

talks.title: Mobile Rules the World - Jump into Mobile AppSec with the OWASP MAS Project
talks.teaser: Walks through the OWASP MAS project, MASVS v2 changes, and the most common flaws found in large-scale mobile app testing.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from the gap between how much time people spend in mobile apps and how little mobile application security testing often receives. It introduces the OWASP Mobile Application Security (MAS) project, including its verification standard, testing guide and checklists, and explains how the mobile attack surface differs from the web. Examples include malicious third-party SDKs and breaches in which a mobile app was used to map back-end systems.

The middle of the talk presents results from an automated benchmark of several thousand popular App Store and Google Play apps, grouped by MASVS control category. Network communication, platform interaction and code quality were among the most frequent failure areas, with many findings traced to third-party libraries and to developers switching off the platforms' built-in secure networking defaults. Storage and cryptography problems were also common. Anti-tampering was presented as a way to raise the effort needed for reverse engineering, not as a fix for underlying flaws. The talk also covered privacy controls being added to MASVS, Apple's privacy labels and manifests, and Google's independent security review program.

For practitioners, the main takeaways are to learn where mobile differs from web, focus testing on the categories with the weakest results, test error conditions and authentication flows, and turn the project's material into developer guidance and training.

talks.title: Unlocking Startup Success: The Vitality of Security Assessments and How to Master Them
talks.teaser: Explains what security assessors look for in early-stage companies and how startups can build basic controls before big customers ask.
talks.summary:
The talk addresses why security posture matters for startups that want to sell to larger customers. The speaker opens with the case of a source code hosting company that lost its business after an attacker reached its admin panel and deleted customer data, and argues that failures like this are avoidable with basic preparation. Assessors generally follow a lifecycle of identification, assessment, protection, monitoring and recovery, and the talk walks through each stage.

The middle section covers threat modeling, third-party risk and open-source components. Vendors are often the weakest point in a company's defenses, so contracts, regular check-ins and audit reports help build customer confidence. The speaker recommends a risk-based approach, using annualized loss expectancy to decide which data needs the strongest controls, and starting from an existing framework such as the NIST Cybersecurity Framework. A hypothetical mobile banking app handling customer identity data serves as a worked example. It covers an asset inventory kept in a spreadsheet, data classification labels, architecture diagrams that include external links, code scanning during build and at runtime, and penetration testing of internet-facing systems.

The closing takeaways are practical. A startup can begin with one designated security person or a part-time advisor, keep its asset inventory and network diagrams current, and consider a SOC 2 Type II report before negotiating large contracts. The session ends with an open question round.

talks.title: Defensive API development techniques for Gophers
talks.teaser: Walks Go developers through hardening HTTP APIs with recovery handlers, rate limiting, fuzzing and JSON Schema validation.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that network controls, packet-inspecting firewalls and API gateways cannot fully remove risk once outside requests reach the application. It frames application-layer hardening for Go APIs as a team effort, where overlapping protections at different layers are acceptable.

A large part covers dependency hygiene. Go's standard library lets services avoid many third-party packages, but adopted libraries should be vetted for project age, release cadence, maintainer responsiveness and transitive dependencies. One case showed an unreleased library with a race condition, forcing a team to pin an untagged commit. Automated update tooling, linters and vulnerability scanners in the pipeline help keep components current. In code, demos showed a recovery handler that keeps the server running after a panic, and a goroutine panic that crashes the process unless it is recovered inside that goroutine. Request inspection covers allowed methods, Content-Type checks, body size limits and rejecting unknown JSON fields. Rate limiting backed by Redis shares state across instances. A fuzzing example on a string-reversing handler surfaced a UTF-8 bug, and JSON Schema constraints for length, pattern, format and enumeration were validated with a library.

The closing takeaways are to understand exposure at each layer, keep dependencies and toolchains updated, make APIs resilient through recovery and rate limits, inspect inputs strictly, fuzz business logic in non-production environments, and feed logs into threshold-based alerts.

talks.title: Fortifying DevOps: Unveiling Security Activities and Maturity Models for Resilient Software Development
talks.teaser: Maps security activities across each DevOps phase and shows how maturity models can measure and guide DevSecOps adoption.
talks.summary:
The talk opens by clearing up common confusion about DevOps, cloud, and the software development lifecycle. The speaker argues that core security principles stay the same whether a team uses waterfall or agile, while the way controls are applied changes. The walkthrough then follows the pipeline from preparation and pre-commit coding through integration, delivery, deployment and operations, pairing each phase with the security tasks that fit it, such as IDE plugins, local scanning, and pipeline-based static analysis.

The middle section compares existing DevSecOps maturity frameworks from GitLab, OWASP and a commercial vendor, and explains why the speaker found them unsatisfying. The alternative is a homegrown five-level scale for each security activity, running from not done, to manual, to automated with offline reports, to alerting on new findings, to failing builds on quality gates. Teams score their applicable activities against targets, and the results roll up into portfolio-level charts for management. Supply chain risk gets focused attention, especially the difference between vulnerable and malicious components, the lack of a standard way to identify malicious packages, and the need to secure the platform, project, pipeline and application layers of CI/CD.

The closing part briefly applies the same lifecycle thinking to AI systems, with threats such as backdoored pre-trained models. It then explains software bills of materials in CycloneDX and SPDX formats as a transparency measure for customers, and suggests digitally signing them alongside binaries. The practical takeaway is to measure maturity per project and to treat build pipelines and dependencies as part of the security scope.

talks.title: Full of SaaS and TOTALLY SECURE
talks.teaser: Explains how unmanaged SaaS sprawl creates security risk and outlines ways to discover and govern shadow IT.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with an analogy: a security team responsible for a building where staff can add doors at will, with no reliable record of the new entrances. The speaker argues that SaaS adoption works the same way. Teams buy and connect applications outside IT, so most organizations cannot produce an accurate inventory of their apps, their users' activity, or their attack surface. Several statistics on shadow IT spending and on employees willing to bypass security guidance frame the problem.

The speaker groups the usual responses into three approaches: ignoring the problem, enabling fast adoption, or locking everything down. Ignoring it invites compromise, and blocking tends to backfire. A behavioral study with Duke University found that punitive or blocking messages drove resentment and workarounds, while a friendly question about why someone adopted a tool earned more cooperation. Incidents discussed include a 2021 Electronic Arts breach that began with stolen Slack session cookies, a 2023 CircleCI breach driven by stolen session tokens, and a Survey Monkey compromise used to send phishing surveys. The talk also covers vendor subprocessors and why smaller firms struggle to recover from breaches.

The recommended path starts with discovery and visibility, followed by automating the research on each app and asking users about new tools through identity provider workflows. Continuous curation should be a named responsibility rather than a one-time project. The speaker closes by urging security teams to help people adopt tools responsibly instead of acting as the department of no.

talks.title: All Day All Night API Security Endpoint Analytics
talks.teaser: Shows how counting API endpoint traffic reveals credential stuffing and bot attacks, with analytics to spot them.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a retailer whose inventory API was being hammered by people checking stock levels so they could strike once shelves were restocked. Jason Kent explains why APIs matter, since they carry the data attackers want. He shows how outsiders find them: reading endpoints from mobile app packages, checking public API docs, probing for exposed GraphQL playgrounds, and spotting old WordPress interfaces.

The core argument is that simply counting requests reveals attacks. Useful measures include requests per endpoint, usernames seen from many IP addresses, user agent versions, origin networks such as residential proxies, and session token age. Baselining normal traffic makes spikes obvious, as when a restaurant chain's peak jumped from about 300,000 to 1.1 million requests per second. Recommended tactics include anomaly detection with machine learning, canary endpoints, and progressive blocking rules rather than permanent IP bans.

The takeaway is that you cannot secure APIs you have not found, so build an inventory and log decrypted traffic in a form you can count. Avoid publishing API specifications, remove dead endpoints, and expect privacy proxies to weaken IP reputation. The Q&A covered retention, with about two weeks of mostly metadata kept, and tuning rules when legitimate traffic gets blocked.

talks.title: Why can't tools automatically fix security vulnerabilities? Or can they?
talks.teaser: Explores why automatic remediation of code vulnerabilities is harder than it looks, and where it can realistically help.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from a common frustration: static analysis scanners report large numbers of findings, and developers often see security checks as friction that slows delivery. The speaker argues that the bottleneck is technology rather than headcount, which makes automated fixing the logical next step, and asks why it has not already been solved.

The middle section tests that idea with fixes that look simple. A SQL injection repair seems trivial, but the database column may be an integer rather than a string, so a generated fix can break the application. Correct fixes also depend on business logic, architecture, organisational coding policy, and whether a flagged issue is actually reachable. An experiment with an AI model on deliberately vulnerable web applications produced usable fixes for only a minority of findings, while many changes touched unrelated code. A live demo showed a scanner result turned into a proposed rule-based fix, which was then committed to a separate branch for testing.

The closing point is that automatic remediation should be limited to well-understood patterns and paired with stronger test coverage, developer involvement and continued security governance. Practitioners should expect partial automation for common bug classes, not wholesale rewrites of vulnerable code.

talks.title: Leave Home Safe: The Good, the Bad, the Ugly
talks.teaser: Walks through a security and privacy audit of Hong Kong's LeaveHomeSafe contact tracing app and its serious flaws.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at LeaveHomeSafe, a covid-19 contact tracing app that Hong Kong required for entry to many public venues from late 2021. The audit was commissioned by a Hong Kong democracy advocacy group, funded by an internet freedom grant, and carried out in spring 2022. Without source code, backend access or valid vaccination QR codes, the testers relied on decompilation, reverse engineering and runtime analysis, which limited coverage but still surfaced several serious problems.

The strengths included secure secret storage in the Android keystore and iOS keychain, cleartext HTTP disabled, restricted Google API keys, and a design that used Firebase device registration to balance exposure alerts with privacy. The weaknesses ranged from screenshots that exposed sensitive screens and task hijacking on older Android versions, to vaccination images left on SD cards and an authentication toggle that could be switched off without any check. The most severe issue was a certificate hostname check that skipped validation for the health system's domain, letting an attacker intercept login credentials and one-time passwords without any warning.

After disclosure, the government called the report inaccurate, yet later quietly patched some issues and removed the authentication feature instead of fixing it. The talk argues that a report with reproducible proof should be checked by an independent third party rather than dismissed by official statements. Practical takeaways include relying on platform defaults, storing secrets in hardware-backed stores, and reviewing TLS validation code carefully before release.

talks.title: Velocity + Safety: Security Metrics All DevOps Should Care About
talks.teaser: Walks through security metrics that engineering teams can use to show risk, velocity and progress alongside DORA measures.
talks.summary:
The talk opens by asking why security metrics are so hard to get right, noting that a podcast discussion on the topic needed about half an hour to reach concrete choices. It argues that metrics should speak to engineers and leadership, not only the security team, and that they can explain strengths, weaknesses and resourcing needs. DORA measures such as deployment frequency, lead time, time to recovery and change failure rate are introduced as a simple model that engineering already understands.

Older approaches come under scrutiny. Count-based figures, raw tool totals and training completion rates are described as lacking context or misleading readers. Newer candidates include environment coverage, control rollout, open findings per control, a security detection rate that should fall as developers learn, mean time to resolve, and exposure windows for accepted risks. A cost view converts earlier fixes into saved developer hours.

Audience questions focused on ranking findings by real business risk and on moving leadership away from vulnerability counts, which the speaker acknowledged is hard in large organizations. Suggested transitions include showing old and new metrics side by side and gradually shrinking the old ones. The takeaway is to tie metrics to velocity and business risk, and to automate data collection so the numbers can be repeated. The talk closes with a product pitch for a centralized platform that gathers that data.

talks.title: State of {Absolute} AppSec
talks.teaser: A live panel weighs where application security stands today, including the promise and risks of AI in the field.
talks.summary:
A live panel recorded in front of a conference audience looks at the state of application security. The hosts of the Absolute AppSec podcast are joined by industry practitioners who share their views on the field. The discussion opens by separating product security from application security. Panelists note that the terms are used inconsistently, and that product security often covers firmware, cloud services and wider enterprise controls.

The middle of the session covers progress and pain points. Panelists credit modern web frameworks with eliminating many classic bug classes, and they point to developer-focused tooling that fits into existing workflows. The struggles they describe include scanners that slow developers down, legacy tools that handle modern JavaScript frameworks poorly, and pentest reports whose advice developers find unclear. They also discuss how shifting security left can push heavy tooling onto developers who were never its intended users. AI gets a long look. Coding assistants are already widespread, and panelists weigh their productivity gains against subtle bugs, data exposure through public platforms, and prompt injection in tools built on language models. A proposed loosening guide, paired with secure-by-default software, draws skepticism.

The closing segment turns forward. Panelists argue that application security teams should stick to fundamentals, treat security as part of the wider software quality effort, and build processes flexible enough to keep pace with new technology. The session makes clear that the field is changing quickly while many of its core communication problems persist.

talks.title: How To Apply DevSecOps Shift-Left Security with OWASP ZAP
talks.teaser: Shows how OWASP ZAP can move web vulnerability testing earlier into the development and CI/CD pipeline.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from the problem that security testing usually arrives late in a traditional delivery pipeline, after software has already reached a test or production environment. The speaker frames shift-left security as a way to move checks closer to developers so they receive findings sooner, and argues this also improves collaboration among development, QA, operations and security staff. He briefly surveys tool categories along the pipeline, including static and composition analysis, dynamic testing, runtime protection, web application firewalls and cloud posture management.

The core of the presentation places ZAP as a proxy between QA testers and the application under test. Traffic produced by routine QA sessions passes through ZAP, which builds a vulnerability report that can go to developers instead of waiting for a separate penetration test. In a demonstration against OWASP Juice Shop, a deliberately vulnerable application, scripts drove a browser through the site while alerts populated in real time. The generated report mapped findings to CWE entries with remediation guidance.

The closing section argues that shift-left reduces remediation cost, speeds deployment, supports cross-functional collaboration and helps with compliance. During questions, the speaker explained that the demo scripts came from a public repository and needed only the target address changed. For practitioners, the takeaway is that existing functional tests can yield security findings when routed through an intercepting proxy.
